Highlight: The mind is a machine for jumping to conclusions, and it is very good at building a coherent story out of far too little evidence.
Note: This is the whole book in one line.

Highlight: System 1 runs automatically and System 2 is normally in a comfortable low-effort mode, in which only a fraction of its capacity is engaged.
A reliable way to make people believe in falsehoods is frequent repetition, because familiarity is not easily distinguished from truth.
Note: Relevant to how I read the news.

Highlight: Nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it.
We are prone to overestimate how much we understand about the world and to underestimate the role of chance in events.
The illusion that we understand the past fosters overconfidence in our ability to predict the future.
Note: Every post-mortem I have ever sat in.

Highlight: Intuition is nothing more and nothing less than recognition.
Skilled intuition develops only in an environment that is sufficiently regular to be predictable, and only with enough practice to learn its regularities.
Note: So expertise is a property of the environment, not just the person.

Highlight: An availability cascade is a self-sustaining chain of events which may start from media reports of a relatively minor event.
The confidence people have in their beliefs is not a measure of the quality of evidence but of the coherence of the story the mind has managed to construct.
Note: Coherence is not evidence. Write this above the desk.

Highlight: Losses loom larger than gains, and the asymmetry between them is roughly two to one.
The brains of humans contain a mechanism that is designed to give priority to bad news.
Odd as it may seem, I am my remembering self, and the experiencing self who does my living is like a stranger to me.
Note: The two selves chapter changed how I plan holidays.

Highlight: A story is about significant events and memorable moments, not about time passing.
When faced with a difficult question we often answer an easier one instead, usually without noticing the substitution.
Note: Substitution. The single most useful idea here.

Highlight: Declarations of high confidence mainly tell you that an individual has constructed a coherent story in his mind, not necessarily that the story is true.
The premortem is a useful exercise: imagine the plan has failed a year from now, and write the history of that disaster.
Note: Try this at the next planning meeting.

Highlight: Algorithms outperform humans in noisy environments for a simple reason: humans are inconsistent in making summary judgments of complex information.
Regression to the mean is a fact of life, and the mind is not built to expect it.
Because adherence to standards is difficult to assess, we substitute the ease with which examples come to mind.
…“The mind is a machine for jumping to conclusions,  and it is very good at building a coherent story out of far too little evidence.”
Design is really an act of communication, which means having a deep understanding of the person with whom the designer is communicating.
Two of the most important characteristics of good design are discoverability and understanding.
Note: Discoverability first. Everything else is downstream.

Highlight: When a device as simple as a door has to come with an instruction manual, even a one-word manual, then it is a failure, poorly designed.
The term affordance refers to the relationship between a physical object and a person. An affordance is a relationship, not a property.
Note: I had this wrong for years.

Highlight: Signifiers signal things, in particular what actions are possible and how they should be done.
Conceptual models are a form of story, resulting from our predisposition to find explanations.
Feedback must be immediate, informative, and planned. Too much of it is as bad as too little.
Note: Every notification system I have ever built violated this.

Highlight: The gulf of evaluation reflects the amount of effort that the person must exert to interpret the physical state of the device.
It is the duty of machines and those who design them to understand people, not the other way around.
When people fail to follow bizarre requirements, they are blamed for the failure. Blaming the person is the wrong response.
Human error usually is a result of poor design: it should be called system error.
Root cause analysis stops too soon. Keep asking why until you reach a fundamental, underlying cause.
Slips occur when the goal is correct but the action performed is wrong. Mistakes occur when the goal itself is wrong.
Note: The taxonomy is the useful part.

Highlight: Knowledge in the world acts as its own reminder, but knowledge in the head is efficient once learned.
Constraints are powerful clues, limiting the set of possible actions.
Forcing functions are a form of physical constraint: failure at one stage prevents the next step from happening.
Natural mapping takes advantage of physical analogies and cultural standards and leads to immediate understanding.
Good design is actually a lot harder to notice than poor design, in part because good designs fit our needs so well that the design is invisible.
Design solves the wrong problem when it starts with the problem as stated. Solve the fundamental problem instead.
Complexity is good; it is confusion that is bad.
“Two of the most important characteristics of good design are discoverability and understanding.”
